titlePl: Matura PR: Człowiek — 180 haseł do gier LingoSpark
titleEn: Matura Extended: People — 180 terms for LingoSpark games
blurbPl: Dział Człowiek na maturę rozszerzoną: tożsamość, charakter, emocje, wartości i dylematy etyczne. Fiszki ENG–PL do wklejenia w LingoSpark.
blurbEn: Extended Matura People module: identity, character, emotions, values and ethical dilemmas. ENG–PL flashcards for LingoSpark.

items.definitionEn: the origins of your family in earlier generations
items.example: Many teenagers start tracing their ancestral roots after a history project.

items.definitionEn: the traditions and history that shape who you are
items.example: She explored her cultural roots through language classes and family stories.

items.definitionEn: a person's rank or status in society
items.example: Social standing should not decide who gets extra help at school.

items.definitionEn: the feeling of belonging to a particular nation
items.example: Sporting events often strengthen a sense of national identity among young people.

items.definitionEn: the feeling that you are accepted as part of a group
items.example: A welcoming school can give newcomers a genuine sense of belonging.

items.definitionEn: the legal status of being a citizen of two countries
items.example: Dual nationality can make it easier to study and work abroad.

items.definitionEn: a mother or father who tries to remove every risk from a child's life
items.example: An overprotective parent may delay a teenager learning to travel alone.

items.definitionEn: the process of learning what kind of person you are
items.example: Travel can speed up self-discovery after secondary school.

items.definitionEn: a difference in attitudes between younger and older people
items.example: Arguments about phones often reveal a generation gap at home.

items.definitionEn: relatives beyond parents and children, such as aunts and grandparents
items.example: In an extended family, childcare is often shared among relatives.

items.definitionEn: a person with no brothers or sisters
items.example: Being an only child can mean more attention but also more pressure.

items.definitionEn: the country where a person or their family comes from
items.example: Refugees are not defined only by their country of origin.

items.definitionEn: the first language a person learns at home
items.example: Writing an essay in your mother tongue feels easier than in a foreign language.

items.definitionEn: able to speak two languages fluently
items.example: A bilingual upbringing can be an advantage on the job market.

items.definitionEn: direct descent from a particular ancestor or family
items.example: She researched her lineage for a school project on local history.

items.definitionEn: a person from whom you are descended
items.example: One forebear of his served as a teacher in the same village.

items.definitionEn: people who are not relatives but give you the support of a family
items.example: For some students a chosen family of friends matters more than relatives.

items.definitionEn: a child legally taken into a family that is not biologically their own
items.example: An adopted child has the same rights as any other member of the family.

items.definitionEn: the mother or father related to a child by birth
items.example: Some adopted teenagers later search for a biological parent.

items.definitionEn: a home in which one parent raises the children
items.example: A single-parent household should not be treated as automatically disadvantaged.

items.definitionEn: the deepest ideas that shape how you judge right and wrong
items.example: Travel made her question some of the core beliefs she grew up with.

items.definitionEn: the class, education and circumstances you grow up in
items.example: Talent should matter more than social background in university admissions.

items.definitionEn: a childhood with wealth, connections or other advantages
items.example: A privileged upbringing does not guarantee maturity or empathy.

items.definitionEn: a family background with little money or status
items.example: The writer often mentions her humble origins in interviews.

items.definitionEn: a person whose behaviour others want to copy
items.example: Young people need a role model who shows honesty, not only success.

items.definitionEn: people of a similar age who influence one another
items.example: A peer group can shape fashion choices more than parents do.

items.definitionEn: a woman's surname before marriage
items.example: Some graduates keep their maiden name for professional publications.

items.definitionEn: the town, region or country you come from
items.example: On the form she wrote her place of origin as a village near Lublin.

items.definitionEn: the ability to understand and manage feelings
items.example: Emotional intelligence matters as much as exam grades in later life.

items.definitionEn: the period of youth that strongly shapes character
items.example: Travel in your formative years can change how you see your own culture.

items.definitionEn: the natural colour and quality of the skin on the face
items.example: A pale complexion is not a sign of poor health in every climate.

items.definitionEn: skin that looks yellowish and unhealthy
items.example: Exam stress left him with a sallow complexion and dark circles.

items.definitionEn: skin that looks rough from age, sun or outdoor work
items.example: Fishermen often have weathered skin after decades at sea.

items.definitionEn: looking younger than your actual age
items.example: Regular sleep can do more for a youthful appearance than expensive creams.

items.definitionEn: looking or becoming old earlier than is typical
items.example: Smoking is a well-known cause of premature ageing.

items.definitionEn: clean, neat and carefully looked after in appearance
items.example: A well-groomed appearance still matters at a formal interview.

items.definitionEn: untidy; not looked after, especially hair or clothes
items.example: An unkempt look can be a fashion choice, not only neglect.

items.definitionEn: facial characteristics that immediately attract attention
items.example: The actress is known less for beauty than for striking features.

items.definitionEn: unusual or easily recognised parts of someone's appearance
items.example: His distinctive features made him easy to spot in a crowd.

items.definitionEn: a body shape that looks fit and strong from sport
items.example: An athletic build does not always mean someone trains every day.

items.definitionEn: a thin, graceful body shape
items.example: The dancer kept a slender figure through years of rehearsal.

items.definitionEn: small and slim, usually used of a woman
items.example: Clothes designed for petite women are still hard to find in many shops.

items.definitionEn: large, strong and heavily built
items.example: A burly security guard stood at the school-gate protest.

items.definitionEn: very thin, especially in the face, often from illness or stress
items.example: After the illness he looked gaunt and tired.

items.definitionEn: physically weak, often because of age or illness
items.example: The frail pensioner needed a ground-floor flat with no stairs.

items.definitionEn: hair that is gradually disappearing from the forehead
items.example: A receding hairline bothered him more than it bothered anyone else.

items.definitionEn: grey hair appearing at the sides of the forehead
items.example: Greying temples made the young teacher look older than she was.

items.definitionEn: very short beard hair that has not been shaved for a day or two
items.example: He arrived at the oral exam with stubble and an unironed shirt.

items.definitionEn: with no beard or moustache
items.example: The school photograph required a clean-shaven look.

items.definitionEn: the way you hold your back and shoulders when sitting or standing
items.example: Hours at a laptop can ruin your posture before you notice.

items.definitionEn: the particular way a person walks
items.example: A confident gait can change how interviewers perceive you.

items.definitionEn: to look similar to another person
items.example: Twins often bear a resemblance to each other even in old age.

items.definitionEn: to get a quality from a parent through genes or example
items.example: You can inherit a trait such as stubbornness without noticing it.

items.definitionEn: medical operations intended to change appearance rather than treat illness
items.example: Teenagers should not treat cosmetic surgery as a shortcut to self-esteem.

items.definitionEn: a complete change of hairstyle, clothes or appearance
items.example: A makeover may boost confidence, but it rarely solves an identity crisis.

items.definitionEn: how you see and feel about the way your body looks
items.example: Social media can distort body image in adolescence.

items.definitionEn: too aware of yourself and worried about being judged
items.example: He felt self-conscious about his accent during the presentation.

items.definitionEn: growing older without desperately hiding the signs of age
items.example: Ageing gracefully is presented in the essay as a form of self-acceptance.

items.definitionEn: hair growing on the face, such as a beard or stubble
items.example: Some workplaces still ban facial hair for hygiene reasons.

items.definitionEn: the habits of keeping yourself clean and tidy
items.example: Personal grooming is a matter of respect in shared accommodation.

items.definitionEn: careful to do your work thoroughly and honestly
items.example: A conscientious student double-checks sources before quoting them.

items.definitionEn: often forgetting things because your mind is on something else
items.example: Even an absent-minded genius still has to meet essay deadlines.

items.definitionEn: willing to consider new ideas and other people's views
items.example: An open-minded listener is more persuasive in a debate than a shouter.

items.definitionEn: unwilling to accept ideas or behaviour different from your own
items.example: A narrow-minded attitude towards other cultures weakens any argument.

items.definitionEn: careful not to say things that will upset or embarrass others
items.example: A tactful comment can criticise an idea without humiliating the speaker.

items.definitionEn: likely to say things that upset people, without intending to
items.example: A tactless joke about someone's family background can ruin a friendship.

items.definitionEn: confident in stating your opinions without being aggressive
items.example: It is possible to be assertive without interrupting others.

items.definitionEn: too ready to obey others and not express your own views
items.example: A submissive classmate may never challenge an unfair group decision.

items.definitionEn: determined not to change your mind, even when you should
items.example: Being stubborn about a first draft rarely improves an essay.

items.definitionEn: having a strong desire to succeed and not giving up easily
items.example: She was determined to pass the oral exam on the first attempt.

items.definitionEn: good at finding practical solutions with limited means
items.example: A resourceful teenager can revise effectively without expensive courses.

items.definitionEn: acting suddenly without thinking about the consequences
items.example: An impulsive comment on social media can cause lasting humiliation.

items.definitionEn: calm and sensible, even in a difficult situation
items.example: A level-headed friend is invaluable during an identity crisis.

items.definitionEn: becoming angry quickly and easily
items.example: A hot-tempered reply in a debate scores no points with examiners.

items.definitionEn: relaxed and not easily upset or worried
items.example: An easy-going roommate makes shared housing far less stressful.

items.definitionEn: friendly and enjoying the company of other people
items.example: Outgoing students often find it easier to start a conversation with strangers.

items.definitionEn: very quiet and not wanting to communicate with others
items.example: A withdrawn pupil may be struggling with self-doubt rather than boredom.

items.definitionEn: slow to show feelings or opinions
items.example: A reserved manner is sometimes mistaken for arrogance.

items.definitionEn: nice to someone in public but unkind or dishonest behind their back
items.example: A two-faced classmate will praise you and then gossip in the group chat.

items.definitionEn: able to be relied on to be honest and keep secrets
items.example: A trustworthy friend does not forward private messages.

items.definitionEn: behaving in a dishonest way in order to trick people
items.example: Deceitful behaviour destroys trust faster than a single argument.

items.definitionEn: too proud of your abilities or appearance
items.example: A conceited winner rarely keeps the respect of the team.

items.definitionEn: not proud; not thinking you are better than others
items.example: A humble apology after a tactless remark can repair a relationship.

items.definitionEn: careful not to cause inconvenience or hurt to others
items.example: A considerate neighbour keeps the volume down after ten.

items.definitionEn: having a personality that attracts and influences others
items.example: A charismatic speaker can still be wrong on the facts.

items.definitionEn: shy and easily frightened; lacking confidence
items.example: A timid student may know the answer but never raise a hand.

items.definitionEn: able to recover quickly from difficulties
items.example: Resilient teenagers treat a failed mock exam as information, not a verdict.

items.definitionEn: able to say clever, amusing things quickly
items.example: A witty remark can defuse tension if it is not sarcastic.

items.definitionEn: eager to find out about things; asking many questions
items.example: An inquisitive mind is an asset in an extended essay, not a nuisance.

items.definitionEn: not friendly or willing to take part; emotionally distant
items.example: Teachers who seem aloof may simply be trying to stay professional.

items.definitionEn: a bitter feeling that you have been treated unfairly
items.example: Long-term resentment towards a sibling often starts with unequal attention.

items.definitionEn: a feeling of great happiness and excitement
items.example: Elation after results day can turn into pressure before the next exam.

items.definitionEn: a strong feeling of shame after being made to look foolish
items.example: Public humiliation is a poor teaching method and a common essay topic.

items.definitionEn: severe mental or emotional pain
items.example: The letter described the anguish of waiting for a medical diagnosis.

items.definitionEn: the complete loss of hope
items.example: Despair after a failed exam is understandable, but it need not last.

items.definitionEn: quiet happiness with what you have
items.example: Contentment is harder to advertise than luxury, yet it appears in many rozprawki.

items.definitionEn: a bittersweet longing for a time in the past
items.example: Nostalgia for childhood can hide how difficult those years actually were.

items.definitionEn: deep regret for something wrong you have done
items.example: Genuine remorse includes changing your behaviour, not only apologising.

items.definitionEn: the unhappy feeling of wanting what someone else has
items.example: Envy of a classmate's marks can either motivate you or poison a friendship.

items.definitionEn: the feeling that someone or something is worthless
items.example: Contempt for people with less education is a form of prejudice.

items.definitionEn: anger because something seems unfair or wrong
items.example: Indignation at online hate speech should lead to action, not only comments.

items.definitionEn: anxiety about something that may happen
items.example: Apprehension before an oral exam is normal; panic is not inevitable.

items.definitionEn: a feeling of excitement and energy
items.example: The exhilaration of performing on stage can surprise even a timid student.

items.definitionEn: intense sorrow, especially after a death or serious loss
items.example: Schools should allow time for grief rather than demanding instant recovery.

items.definitionEn: the comfortable feeling when something unpleasant stops or does not happen
items.example: There was audible relief in the hall when the exam paper looked familiar.

items.definitionEn: annoyed disappointment because you cannot achieve something
items.example: Frustration with a language plateau is common at B2.

items.definitionEn: sadness because something was not as good as you hoped
items.example: Disappointment after a mock exam can still be useful feedback.

items.definitionEn: a feeling of awkward shame in front of others
items.example: Embarrassment about an accent often disappears after a month abroad.

items.definitionEn: great surprise
items.example: The class listened in astonishment when the quietest pupil won the debate.

items.definitionEn: lasting anger and disappointment about unfair treatment
items.example: Bitterness about a lost opportunity can freeze personal growth.

items.definitionEn: a strong wish for someone or something you do not have
items.example: A longing for independence often clashes with family ties.

items.definitionPl: trwoga, przerażenie na myśl o czymś
items.definitionEn: great fear about something that will happen
items.example: Sunday-evening dread before school is more common than students admit.

items.definitionEn: both positive and negative emotions about the same thing
items.example: Leavers often have mixed feelings about leaving a familiar school.

items.definitionEn: to accept a difficult situation and learn to live with it
items.example: It took him a year to come to terms with moving to another city.

items.definitionEn: to hide your feelings instead of expressing them
items.example: People who bottle up anger often explode over a trivial remark.

items.definitionEn: to be deeply affected by criticism or a remark
items.example: Try not to take something to heart if the comment was never about you.

items.definitionEn: to become suddenly very angry
items.example: If you lose your temper in a discussion, you usually lose the argument too.

items.definitionEn: to stay calm and in control of your behaviour
items.example: If you keep your composure during follow-up questions, examiners notice.

items.definitionEn: feeling unable to cope because there is too much to deal with
items.example: First-year students often feel overwhelmed by conflicting expectations.

items.definitionEn: feeling guilty to an extreme, constant degree
items.example: A guilt-ridden apology is still empty if the behaviour does not change.

items.definitionEn: confidence in your own worth and abilities
items.example: Constant comparison on social media can damage self-esteem.

items.definitionEn: the sense that you deserve respect, independent of success
items.example: Grades should not be the only measure of self-worth.

items.definitionEn: a period of confusion about who you are and what you want
items.example: An identity crisis in late adolescence is more common than textbooks admit.

items.definitionEn: knowledge of your own character, feelings and motives
items.example: Self-awareness helps you notice when prejudice is shaping a first impression.

items.definitionEn: the ability to recognise your flaws without hating yourself
items.example: Self-acceptance is not the same as refusing to change.

items.definitionEn: the feeling that you are not good enough or may fail
items.example: A little self-doubt can improve an essay; too much can freeze it.

items.definitionEn: a lasting belief that you are less valuable than others
items.example: An inferiority complex can hide behind jokes and arrogance.

items.definitionEn: anxiety about identity and purpose in middle age
items.example: The novel treats a midlife crisis as a chance to reinvent yourself, not a joke.

items.definitionEn: to become less shy and more willing to talk to people
items.example: Drama club can help you come out of your shell before the oral exam.

items.definitionPl: odnaleźć się na nowo, zmienić swoje życie
items.definitionEn: to change your image, habits or career in a significant way
items.example: University is often the first chance to reinvent yourself away from home.

items.definitionEn: the process of improving your character, skills or self-knowledge
items.example: Travel can support personal growth if you do more than collect photos.

items.definitionEn: a struggle between two feelings, values or desires inside you
items.example: Inner conflict between loyalty and honesty is a classic rozprawka theme.

items.definitionEn: the ability to make yourself work or behave well without being forced
items.example: Self-discipline matters more in revision than last-minute panic.

items.definitionEn: the ability to depend on your own efforts rather than on others
items.example: Self-reliance should not mean refusing every offer of help.

items.definitionEn: not believing in your own abilities
items.example: A lack of confidence can look like laziness to an impatient teacher.

items.definitionEn: the feeling that your success is undeserved and you will be found out
items.example: Impostor syndrome is common among high-achieving students.

items.definitionPl: rachunek sumienia, głębokie zastanowienie nad sobą
items.definitionEn: careful, honest thinking about your motives and values
items.example: A year of soul-searching followed her decision to change schools.

items.definitionEn: the feeling that your life has a meaningful direction
items.example: Volunteering gave him a sense of purpose after a period of self-doubt.

items.definitionEn: to achieve as much as you are capable of
items.example: A good teacher helps you fulfil your potential instead of chasing rankings.

items.definitionEn: to be as good as people hoped or demanded
items.example: Some teenagers refuse to live up to expectations that were never theirs.

items.definitionEn: to act according to your own values rather than other people's wishes
items.example: It is hard to be true to yourself in a peer group that rewards conformity.

items.definitionEn: the influence of people your age to behave in a certain way
items.example: Peer pressure can push someone into cruelty they would never choose alone.

items.definitionPl: osoba, która za wszelką cenę chce się przypodobać
items.definitionEn: someone who tries too hard to make others like them, often at a cost to themselves
items.example: A people-pleaser rarely states an unpopular but honest opinion.

items.definitionEn: a situation in which you feel safe and unchallenged
items.example: Language learning starts when you leave your comfort zone.

items.definitionEn: the idea you have of your own character and appearance
items.example: A distorted self-image can survive even after compliments.

items.definitionEn: pride in yourself that stops you accepting bad treatment
items.example: Self-respect means walking away from a friendship based on humiliation.

items.definitionEn: a lack of confidence about yourself or your relationships
items.example: Insecurity about looks is heavily marketed to teenagers.

items.definitionEn: the state of being open to emotional hurt
items.example: Showing vulnerability can deepen a friendship instead of weakening it.

items.definitionEn: the habit of feeling sorry for yourself in an unhelpful way
items.example: Self-pity after one bad mark can become an excuse to stop trying.

items.definitionEn: to recover quickly after a setback
items.example: The ability to bounce back after rejection is a form of resilience.

items.definitionEn: the quality of being honest and sticking to your moral principles
items.example: Integrity means citing sources even when nobody is checking.

items.definitionEn: an unfair opinion formed without enough knowledge or experience
items.example: Prejudice against an accent is still prejudice, even if it is unspoken.

items.definitionEn: the ability to understand and share another person's feelings
items.example: Empathy is a skill that can be practised, not only a personality trait.

items.definitionEn: an oversimplified idea about a whole group of people
items.example: A stereotype about only children is a weak foundation for an essay.

items.definitionEn: willingness to accept behaviour and beliefs different from your own
items.example: Tolerance does not require you to agree; it requires you not to humiliate.

items.definitionEn: stubborn and unfair dislike of people who are different
items.example: The article condemned bigotry in online comments.

items.definitionEn: a hidden preference that affects judgement without you noticing
items.example: Unconscious bias can influence who gets chosen as class representative.

items.definitionEn: a rule applied more strictly to one group than to another
items.example: A double standard about emotions still tells boys not to show grief.

items.definitionEn: a situation in which two ethical principles clash and both choices hurt someone
items.example: Reporting a friend for cheating is a classic moral dilemma in school essays.

items.definitionEn: a difficult choice between two courses of action that both have moral costs
items.example: An ethical dilemma about telling the truth appears in many matura prompts.

items.definitionEn: the inner sense of what is right and wrong
items.example: A guilty conscience after a lie is a sign that your values still work.

items.definitionEn: claiming high moral standards while doing the opposite
items.example: Hypocrisy is easy to spot when a campaigner for kindness is cruel online.

items.definitionEn: unselfish concern for other people's welfare
items.example: Altruism in a peer group can be as contagious as mockery.

items.definitionEn: a responsibility you have as a member of society
items.example: Voting can be seen as a civic duty rather than a personal hobby.

items.definitionEn: the idea that every person deserves respect simply for being human
items.example: Poverty should never be treated as a reason to deny someone human dignity.

items.definitionEn: to treat a person or group as shameful or unworthy
items.example: Schools must not stigmatise pupils who receive extra learning support.

items.definitionEn: to defend a person, idea or right, especially when it is unpopular
items.example: It takes moral courage to stand up for a classmate others mock.

items.definitionEn: to think you are better than someone else
items.example: It is easy to look down on people whose upbringing was poorer than yours.

items.definitionPl: przymykać oko, udawać, że się nie widzi
items.definitionEn: to ignore something wrong that you know is happening
items.example: Teachers who turn a blind eye to mockery teach that cruelty is acceptable.

items.definitionEn: to state your position clearly and refuse to stay neutral
items.example: At some point you have to take a stand instead of collecting likes.

items.definitionEn: shared opinions or interests that make agreement possible
items.example: A good debate finds common ground before it lists disagreements.

items.definitionEn: the bravery to do what is right despite criticism or risk
items.example: Moral courage is quieter than heroism and more useful in everyday life.

items.definitionEn: to act against your own moral beliefs for an advantage
items.example: Do not compromise your principles for a higher mark or a louder peer group.

items.definitionEn: to keep feeling angry with someone for a long time after they hurt you
items.example: People who hold a grudge rarely notice how much it costs them.

items.term: put yourself in someone else's shoes
items.definitionEn: to imagine how another person feels in their situation
items.example: Before you judge, try to put yourself in someone else's shoes.

items.definitionEn: the principles that guide your own choices and behaviour
items.example: A gap year can test whether your personal values survive outside school.

items.definitionEn: a situation in which two people or groups you care about want opposite things
items.example: Conflicting loyalties between friends and family appear in many oral-exam stories.

items.definitionEn: the tendency not to help because you assume someone else will
items.example: The bystander effect explains why a whole corridor can ignore humiliation.

items.definitionEn: strong public disapproval attached to a person, condition or group
items.example: The social stigma around mental-health struggles still silences teenagers.

items.definitionEn: to behave towards people in a way that recognises their worth
items.example: The simplest ethical rule in a classroom is to treat others with respect.
